summary: Jon Postel's proposal for a person to hand out official socket numbers for standard protocols and publish where host-specific services can be found. He suggests ranges for network-wide standard functions, host-specific functions, reserved numbers and experiments. Initial assignments include Telnet, File Transfer, Remote Job Entry, Echo and Discard. It was replaced by RFC 433.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 349 proposes that one administrator assign official socket numbers for standard protocols and publish the assignments. It also suggests ranges for standard, host-specific, reserved, and experimental functions.

subtitle: A proposal for assigning ARPANET socket numbers to standard services.

tldr.problem: Standard protocols needed official socket numbers, and users needed a published list of numbers for host-specific services.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes a central socket-number administrator, four allocation ranges, and initial numbers for five network-wide functions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 349 is a proposal for socket-number assignments and was obsoleted by RFC 433.

today: RFC 349 proposed socket-number assignments and was obsoleted by RFC 433.

sections.title: Coordinating Socket Numbers
sections.content:
Jon Postel proposes that a central administrator hand out official socket numbers for standard protocols. The administrator would also track and publish socket numbers where host-specific services could be found.

The memo relates these decimal socket numbers to the socket called L in the official Initial Connection Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal gives one person responsibility for assigning service numbers and keeping a public list. That way, the numbers for standard services could be coordinated.

sections.title: Proposed Ranges and Assignments
sections.content:
The proposed ranges are 0-63 for network-wide standard functions, 64-127 for host-specific functions, 128-239 reserved for future use, and 240-255 for experimental functions.

Initial proposed assignments within the network-wide range are socket 1 for Telnet, 3 for File Transfer, 5 for Remote Job Entry, 7 for Echo, and 9 for Discard.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal divides socket numbers into four ranges. It assigns example numbers to five services, including Telnet, File Transfer, Echo, and Discard.

sections.title: Proposal Status
sections.content: RFC 349 presents a proposal: it says that an administrator should issue numbers and that the listed values are initial allocations. The unit metadata records RFC 433 as the later document that obsoleted it.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo proposes a system for assigning socket numbers. A later RFC replaced the proposal.

references.text: Postel, J., "Arpanet Official Protocol Standards", RFC 322, March 1972.
